extracted.intended_audience: educated early-18th-century readers / coffee-house society (Spectator readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Short didactic essays advising readers on social conduct, manners, and style (conversation, behaviour in public rooms, reading of prayers, and responses to beauty and affectation) as published in The Spectator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not obtrude personal cares in company
rubrics_metrics.description: Cares, Distresses, Diseases, Uneasinesses, and Dislikes of our own, are by no means to be obtruded upon our Friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The part of life called Conversation is an indulgence to the sociable part of our make and we should bring our proportion of good will or good humour among friends rather than trouble them with relations that oblige them to affliction. Examples/anti-patterns: valetudinarians who complain in company should be sent home; personal ailments belong to a physician, not to a public company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring cheerfulness to social gatherings
rubrics_metrics.description: That Part of Life ... is an Indulgence to the Sociable Part of our Make; and should incline us to bring our Proportion of good Will or good Humour among the Friends we meet with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep up the cheerfulness of spirits and never let them sink below an inclination to be well-pleased. Practical means: keep bodies in exercise and minds at ease; avoid adding 'spleen' or ill-humour to life's natural misfortunes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valetudinarians should refrain from speaking of themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Valetudinarians should be sworn before they enter into Company, not to say a Word of themselves till the Meeting breaks up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chronic complainers or those always lamenting their health are inappropriate company and their self-disclosures are an obligation on others; keep such complaints private.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate an equality of mind (avoid extremes of joy or sorrow)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is as mean to be overjoyed upon Occasions of Good-Fortune, as to be dejected in Circumstances of Distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a steady temper where neither transport nor weeping are habitual responses; ambition, envy and impertinent mirth disturb this balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contentment as a preservative of health and tranquillity
rubrics_metrics.description: To be anxious for nothing but what Nature demands as necessary ... this Temper will preserve Health in the Body, as well as Tranquility in the Mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the example of Cottilus—contentment with necessities avoids many evils of life. Practical advice: avoid needless ambition and desires beyond natural needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical resignation reduces fear of pain and death
rubrics_metrics.description: Uranius ... is so thoroughly persuaded of another Life, and endeavours so sincerely to secure an Interest in it, that he looks upon Pain but as a quickening of his Pace to an Home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopting a belief in another life and religious resignation can make pain and sickness less affecting; view death as a passage rather than an end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not be seduced by mere outward beauty or affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not indeed to be denied, that there is something irresistible in a Beauteous Form; ... People can bear any Quality in the World better than Beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that beauty is a 'possession foreign to them' and transient; cure over-attachment to beauty by attention and judgment. Anti-pattern: admiring beauty as a merit rather than a gift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize types of beauty and their social effects (beware artifice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various female types — Amaryllis (natural simplicity), Dulcissa (beauty by art), Merab (wit undermined by affectation), Albacinda (familiarity as a lure), Eudosia (commanding beauty), Eucratia (feminine goodness), Omnamante (innocent aspect hiding vice) — show different dangers and virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing persons, note whether charm is natural or manufactured; beware those whose behaviour (affectation, artful familiarity, deceit) corrodes true merit. Examples: Dulcissa's artifice, Merab's affectation destroying both wit and beauty, Omnamante's innocent aspect masking perfidy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not value yourself for transient qualities (warning to the beautiful)
rubrics_metrics.description: What, said the Philosopher, could that Image of yours say for it self if it could speak? ... 'That it is very Beautiful.' And are not you ashamed ... to value your self upon that only of which a Piece of Brass is capable?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty is like a piece of brass — a hollow ground for vanity if taken as the sole basis of self-worth; cultivate qualities beyond appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using wealth to pose as learning (don't wager to prove knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are … young Fellows … who wager themselves into Statesmen, Historians, Geographers, Mathematicians, and every other Art, when the Persons with whom they talk have not Wealth equal to their Learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: staking money to silence or bully interlocutors and thereby creating an appearance of learning. Advice: genuine learning is not purchased by wagers; such behaviour is a compendious (shortcut) and pernicious way to pose as wise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe public-room etiquette: limit disruptive singing/whistling
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide the Spaces of a Publick Room, and certify Whistlers, Singers, and Common Orators, that are heard further than their Portion of the Room comes to, that the Law is open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not act as if in an empty room; maintain decorum and keep one's voice/activity within one's allotted portion so as not to interrupt lawful discourse. Treat habitual noisy performers as trespassers in public conversational spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in dress and fashion (avoid extreme forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: We have conformed our selves to your Rules, even to our very Dress. There is not one of us but has reduced our outward Petticoat to its ancient Sizable Circumference ... but 'tis on Condition, Mr. SPECTATOR extends not his Censure so far.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encouraged: moderation (reducing exaggerated fashions). Observation: fashions are mutually imitated across sexes (men's coats mimicking women's petticoats); aim for regular figure rather than grotesque extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read Common Prayer with clarity, emphasis and fervour
rubrics_metrics.description: The well Reading of the Common Prayer is of so great Importance ... I heard the Service read so distinctly, so emphatically, and so fervently, that it was next to an Impossibility to be unattentive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifics: read with clearness, loudness, and strength; learn to speak deliberately; place emphasis and give proper accent to each word; vary the voice according to the nature of the sentence. Avoid folding arms, lolling on the book, reading too fast, and 'Pindarick' irregularity (pronouncing some words with excessive deliberation then rushing others). Training: propose a model reader at clergy assemblies to set an example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affected or irregular reading styles ('Pindarick' readers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pindarick Readers ... pronounce five or six Words with great Deliberation, and the five or six subsequent ones with as great Celerity: The first part of a Sentence with a very exalted Voice, and the latter part with a submissive one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for evenness of voice and delivery; steady pace and consistent tone are preferable to sudden, theatrical alternations which confuse meaning and distract the congregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not avoid fervent religious diction for fear of 'cant'
rubrics_metrics.description: This Indifferency seems to me to arise from the Endeavour of avoiding the Imputation of Cant ... Cant ... signifies all sudden Exclamations, Whinings, unusual Tones, and in fine all Praying and Preaching, like the unlearned of the Presbyterians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish true fervour and appropriate emphasis in devotional reading from mere whining or affected tones; do not let fear of being accused of 'cant' prevent a moving and reverent delivery of prayer.
